item.content:encoded:
Was Brandon Newport Framed by Dr. Yvonne Pierpont? Part 2
Part 2 examines the locked folder only she saw, the life coach who secretly recorded him, and the forensic questions police never pursued.
Part 1 laid out the case: Dr. Yvonne Pierpont’s accusation that her husband, Delta pilot Brandon Newport, drugged and sexually assaulted her; his denial; a “confession” he says she coached, after telling him to confess or she would divorce him; lab results that settle nothing; and a police investigation that tested his story but not hers.
Since May 19, 2026, Newport has been in the Pinellas County Jail, awaiting trial.
More charges followed. One for violating an injunction. Six for possessing child pornography. He denies them all.
Part 3 will examine those charges.
In jail, Newport says, a scan showed that the cancer he had spent two years fighting had returned. He has chondrosarcoma, a bone cancer in the pelvis. Newport says his Mayo Clinic oncologist warned that without surgery, he could die within a year.
He cannot get to the surgeons at Mayo from a jail cell.
A PILOT, A VETERAN, A PRISONER
Newport is 41. He says he joined the Army in 2005 and served in Kuwait, Iraq, and Afghanistan. He came home a veteran, rated 100 percent disabled from his service.
He went to Texas A&M, taught flying at the Florida Institute of Technology, and became a Delta pilot.
He was also a Federal Flight Deck Officer, trained and deputized by Homeland Security to carry a gun in the cockpit.
Then cancer grounded him. He fought it for two years. Newport says his doctors did not expect him to fly again. On April 22, 2026, he flew for Delta again.
He had been back at work for four weeks. Then, a few houses from home, St. Petersburg police stopped his pickup truck and arrested him for sexual battery.
Much of the following account comes from his wife's statements to St. Petersburg police detective Dagni Closser in March 2026.
2023: SHE TELLS HIM TO MOVE OUT
Pierpont told Closser that during a Thanksgiving 2023 camping trip, she awoke to Newport "sodomizing" her. She said she ordered him to leave their home. He moved into a rental house that November.
Two months later, in January 2024, doctors found aggressive cancer in his pelvis.
Pierpont was a Mayo Clinic surgeon. She told police she found him "help with the right doctors." He spent two years relearning to walk.
THE LOCKED FOLDER
In February 2025, acting on what she called a “gut feeling,” Pierpont examined Newport’s iPad without asking him.
The folder was locked. She knew his passcode. She opened it.
Pierpont told police the folder contained videos showing her and another woman, both apparently unconscious, being sexually abused. She also described photographs of fully clothed young girls in public places.
She told police she sent the videos and photos to herself.
She texted him photos of clothed girls in public places, which is not a crime. He denied wrongdoing. She did not send him the video she says showed him abusing her while she was unconscious, which would be one. By her account, she never confronted him about that video at all.
Shame or shock might explain it. But it means the most serious thing she says she found is the one thing no one else has ever seen.
Pierpont said he caught her looking through the iPad. They argued.
The police report says that Newport then took her laptop and “presumably deletes everything she had saved in the cloud.”
“Presumably.” No one says they saw him delete anything.
The photos survived because she had texted them to him. She says the videos were lost.
Yet she says she had sent the videos to herself. Files sent that way usually leave copies: on the phone that receives them, on the servers in between, and in a deleted-items folder for 30 days.
Police seized 11 of Newport’s devices in May. The available file identifies no recovered video depicting Pierpont or the other woman.
The file shows no forensic examination of the iPad for the folder Pierpont described. It shows no request for her Apple records. Either could show whether the folder existed, and whether anything was deleted.
Newport says there was no folder. "She just completely made it up," he said.
No one but Pierpont says they saw the videos of her or the other woman.
HER BROTHER'S PLAN
Pierpont did not initially go to the police. She went to her brother, Brandon Pierpont, who warned her that divorce would likely give Newport partial custody of the boys.
The advice, as Closser later documented it, was explicit: "It was recommended that she will allow Brandon to think they are getting back together and therefore she can control Brandon's interactions with the children."
She told Newport she needed a year to "reflect." There were rules. He could not live in the house. He had to leave by 9:30 p.m. No electronics at home or at the boys' games.
THE COACH WHO RECORDED HIM
Around then, Newport began working with Sarah Eva Michielson, a life coach who describes herself as an "attachment theory coach."
But Pierpont met Michielson first, in a therapy group. Michielson told police she offered to help Newport.
In one Zoom session, according to the detective, Newport asked whether HIPAA protected what he said. Michielson told him, "Sure." She was secretly recording him.
What he told Michielson, she told his wife.
She called herself his coach. In reality, she was his wife's spy.
At her first meeting with Detective Closser on March 3, Pierpont repeated what Michielson had told her: Newport had been "kicked out of the dark web." Eight days later, Closser interviewed Michielson.
Michielson told the detective that Newport admitted to masturbating to a video of a 12-year-old girl, fully clothed, ice skating.
Closser listened to Michielson's recording. She wrote: "I heard him specifically say he had not masturbated to her."
Closser's word for Michielson's statements was "inconsistent."
Police did not ask why the coach told them something her own tape contradicted. They kept building the case.
Newport says he paid Michielson for the sessions, and that she presented herself as a therapist. She told police she is not a licensed therapist. On her own recording, when Newport asked whether their talks were protected under HIPAA, she told him, “Sure.”
In Florida, where Newport was, practicing therapy without a license is a felony. Whether coaching him over Zoom from Wisconsin crosses that line is a question no one has yet asked.
PIERPONT SAID SHE FEARED NEWPORT
Pierpont told police she felt unsafe and believed he should not be alone with their sons.
By her account, she had watched a video of her husband abusing her. She did not seek a divorce. She did not go to the police.
The family's routine continued. Newport came to the house each night to put the boys to bed. He says that while Pierpont worked in Wisconsin, he cared for them alone for two weeks of every month.
Newport says the arrangement continued for more than three years, both before and after she says she found the folder. Several friends have confirmed it.
She also told Closser that in May 2025 she woke with her shirt pulled up and Newport "looming over" her.
She still did not go to the police.
Newport said he was looking for his cancer medication, which she kept at the house. He said he had told her he was coming over. "It is a complete falsehood," he said.
A private hair test later found Ambien from about that time. Newport says Ambien prescribed in his name was meant for her, and that she took it. Police found a prescription bottle in the house filled on May 7, 2025, the same month.
DECEMBER 23
Newport cooked dinner on December 23, 2025.
By her own account, she already believed he had drugged her and abused her in her sleep. She ate the dinner he cooked anyway.
At bedtime, Pierpont felt "overwhelmingly tired." She said she believed he had drugged her food.
Her son was asleep beside her. Pierpont did not call 911 or leave the room. She did not wake anyone or move the child. She turned on her phone's recorder, placed it face down on the nightstand, and went to sleep.
She says the recording captured sounds of masturbation. Newport says it is her snoring.
Pierpont told police Newport admitted the following day that he had raised her shirt, masturbated beside her, and "finished on" their son's comforter.
That evening, some 22 hours after the dinner, on December 24, Pierpont underwent a sexual assault examination at the Suncoast Center in St. Petersburg. Pierpont did not make a police report. Her examination kit went to a state laboratory in Tallahassee and sat untested.
TEN WEEKS
For the next 10 weeks, Pierpont gathered evidence instead of going to police. She did three things. First, she secretly recorded him at a restaurant.
She told police that on the recording, Newport admitted giving her melatonin, not Ambien. Melatonin is an over-the-counter sleep aid. She told police he denied having sex with her, but said he would have if she had been in a better position.
The police file does not show that the detective ever heard that recording.
Second, she had her hair tested. Pierpont's brother arranged a private hair analysis. It reported no Ambien corresponding to December, the month of the alleged assault.
Third, she weighed a deal. A civil lawyer suggested a possible agreement over the children. Closser wrote that they "could offer to leave out all of the criminal activity he has been doing if he agrees to all of her parameters with the kids."
The file does not show whether that proposal became an offer. Newport said she never made such an offer.
Pierpont gave police two explanations for delaying reporting him.
She told them she was afraid that reporting would lead to "Brandon getting access to their children," and her brother had told her the laboratory would not test her examination kit without a police report.
Her second explanation does not match Florida law. A victim can request testing of her kit without a police report. Pierpont did not ask.
Neither does her first, if Newport is telling the truth: He says she kept leaving the boys alone with him in Florida two weeks a month, right up to his arrest, while she worked at the Mayo Clinic in Wisconsin.
He says he also made meals three times a day until the day of his arrest.
MARCH 2026: SHE GOES TO POLICE
On March 2, 2026, Pierpont went to the police. She said she had recordings and other evidence that Newport had been drugging her.
Pierpont told Closser she planned a “disclosure” session with Newport. Police had been told it was one “in which he is supposed to talk about his deviances and what he had been doing, criminally, to her.”
She proposed having the life coach, Michielson, listen.
Closser advised against involving a third party. Instead, she proposed a controlled call in which Pierpont would speak with Newport while the detective secretly recorded the conversation.
Pierpont did not want the controlled call, which would have given police their own recording.
Closser decided Pierpont could record Newport herself. That left Pierpont in control of the recording and what the police received. The detective was not there. Pierpont secretly recorded a five-hour session with Newport.
She gave a recording to police. Newport says it was an edited copy, not the original.
Pierpont never gave the detectives the original recording. A third party edited the recording and made changes to the recording, highlighting the "relevant parts of the recording," and then uploaded it to evidence.com.
WHAT HE THOUGHT IT WAS
Newport thought the “disclosure” session would help save his marriage.
The word comes from marriage counseling after infidelity: one spouse tells the other everything he has done, often with a therapist present, so the couple can start over on the truth. Newport says that is what he was told this was. He says a therapist was supposed to be there. She was not.
He says Pierpont set the terms. He was to admit every wrong he had done in the marriage. If he refused, she would file for divorce at once. He says he believed that if he got through it, they would have a chance to begin again.
He did not know she had gone to the police. He did not know a detective had told her she could record him. He did not know he was being recorded.
He says she told him beforehand what she needed to hear. “I need you to say that you put stuff in my chicken,” he says she told him.
THE CONFESSION AND THE LAB
The State's case rests heavily on that recording. In her summary, Closser reported that Newport admitted putting 5 mg of Ambien in Pierpont's chicken, touching her and ejaculating "on her stomach and her vagina."
Five milligrams is the standard starting dose of Ambien prescribed for women. It is meant to help someone fall asleep, not to keep them unconscious.
The Pinellas County crime laboratory also contradicts the story:
No semen was detected on the tested swabs, including those collected from Pierpont's navel and genitals, or on the underwear she submitted.
The lab detected male DNA on her cervical and vaginal swabs, but too little to identify whose. A trace like that cannot show how or when it got there. It does not prove penetration, and it does not rule it out.
Newport's DNA was detected on Pierpont's breast, pubic area, buttocks, and the waistband of her underwear. The couple was married, and Newport says they had intimate contact when she was awake that night but did not have intercourse.
The sample from Pierpont's buttocks contained DNA from three contributors: Pierpont, Newport, and an unidentified person.
DNA from an unidentified male was detected on Pierpont's navel. The laboratory excluded Newport as its source. According to the detective, Newport's "confession" said he ejaculated on her stomach. The male DNA found there was not his.
Her blood and urine were tested. The lab detected zolpidem, the active ingredient in Ambien. But the report did not say whether it came from blood or urine, or how much was present.
Newport says she took Ambien on her own, from prescriptions in his name.
TWO STORIES, NO SEMEN
Pierpont gave police two versions of the same act.
First, she told Closser that on December 24, the day after, Newport told her he "finished on" their son's comforter.
Then came the March recording. According to the detective's summary, Newport said he ejaculated "on her stomach and her vagina."
The comforter, or her body. The record does not say which.
Either way, there should have been semen somewhere. The lab found none on her: not on her stomach, not on her genitals, not on her underwear. The comforter, the one place she first said it went, was never tested.
Newport says neither happened and that she coached the confession on tape and he said it to save their marriage.
WHAT NO ONE TESTED
Pierpont told police she wore a sports bra, shirt, sweatshirt, sweatpants, and underwear. Her examination kit held a gray bra, a Christmas sweater, and blue leggings. The lab tested her underwear. The file shows no testing of the bra, the sweater, or the leggings.
Two blankets from her exam went into evidence, and police collected a third blanket on March 4. The file shows no lab test of any of them.
Pierpont told police Newport had said he "finished on" their son's comforter, which meant he had ejaculated on it.
Blankets from her exam went into evidence. The file shows no lab test of any of them.
Semen can remain detectable on fabric for weeks. Testing the comforter could have supported her account, or undercut it. The file does not say whether investigators collected that comforter.
She saved her dinner. The county lab told Closser it “would not meet criteria to be analyzed.” The food had been in Pierpont’s hands for three months. She had her hair tested at a private lab. She never had the food tested. And when the county lab said no, nothing in the file shows police tried anywhere else.
Add it up. They never tested the clothes she described. The blankets were never tested. Her dinner was never tested. Her iPad folder was never examined. Her cloud records were never requested. Her phone was never searched.
Every one of those tests could have confirmed her story or undercut it. Police ran none of them. They tested his bank accounts, his crypto accounts, and his phone.
That is not an investigation of what happened that night. It is an investigation of him.
SHE KEPT EATING HIS COOKING
Newport says he cooked and cleaned and kept the house. He says Pierpont and the boys ate his meals and drank his milkshakes from December 23 until the night before his arrest. His father and friends saw it, he says, and can confirm it.
If he is telling the truth, she believed her husband drugged her food, and she kept eating it for five months. She also let her sons eat it.
On May 18, he says she ate the dinner he cooked. Police arrested him the next morning.
WHAT SHE STOOD TO GAIN
I do not know whether Pierpont is telling the truth. I do know she had reasons to want Newport out of her life and her sons' lives.
The first reason is custody. A divorce could give Newport partial custody. Florida law also starts from an equal split of marital property. A typical divorce would likely give him about half.
A man in jail does not get partial custody. Newport says that in their divorce, she is asking for full custody of their two sons and 100 percent of their property.
There was also the matter of life insurance. Pierpont was the beneficiary of coverage worth several million dollars.
THE TIMING
The brother's plan came in February 2025, while Newport was sick. Pierpont went to the police in March 2026 as he recovered.
On April 22, 2026, he returned to Delta. Newport says that within a day of his return to Delta, Pierpont accessed his employee benefits account and increased his life-insurance coverage to the maximum available amount.
Newport recalls Pierpont telling him: "You never know if cancer comes back." He describes two additional transactions: an April 30 property listing on which she signed his name without authorization, and a transfer of 51 percent of a rental property to her mother about two weeks before his arrest.
Four weeks after he went back to work, he was in jail.
Now, Newport says, the cancer is back. He cannot get to the surgeons who saved him the first time. His doctor, he says, warned that without surgery he could die within a year.
If he dies in jail, there will be no trial. Pierpont keeps the boys. She keeps the property. And, if Newport is right about the insurance, she collects the maximum.
No one has to intend that outcome for it to happen. But no one at the St. Petersburg Police Department asked who stood to gain.
QUESTIONS
Why did police never examine the iPad for the folder Pierpont described?
Why did they never ask Apple for her cloud records?
Why were the clothes she described, and the blankets, never tested?
Why did the detective accept her refusal of a controlled call?
Why did police not question a coach whose statement contradicted her own recording?
What changed between April, when the lead detective found no probable cause for child pornography, and August, when the State filed six counts?
Why did police not run the DNA of the other man found on Pierpont's naval to determine who else may have been with her that night?
None of this establishes that Pierpont fabricated her allegations.
Delayed reporting, continued contact, and private evidence gathering can all occur in genuine abuse cases.
The unanswered question is whether police subjected the competing accounts, and the motives of the people offering them, to equal scrutiny.
Part 3 will examine what police found in Newport's home. And what they did not.
Disclosure: People who support Brandon Newport hired me. I agreed to publish what I find, regardless of which side it favors. The disclosure is in Part 1.

item.content:encoded:
Nick Cannon is "always open" to getting back together with Mariah Carey.
The Masked Singer host married the Hero hitmaker in 2008 and though they divorced in 2016, he revealed they speak "almost every day" about their 15-year-old twins Moroccan and Monroe and he still regards her as his "greatest friend".
He told Us Weekly magazine: "We talk almost every day or every other day, specifically just about the kids. We were laughing about [reports we’re not close]. I was like, 'Who is telling people that?'
"On the flip side, I’ve heard we’re getting back together. I’ll deliver the truth with the doc. I’m always open [to that].
"Our divorce wasn’t messy. We were able to move on and be the best parents we can.
"I always say Mariah Carey was my greatest friend and my greatest teacher. What I learned most from her is how to hold on to what’s true and create your own spaces, without letting outside energy infiltrate.
"I’ve never seen somebody operate on their own frequency, and it’s always so positive. And you know all that she’s been through in her life. I think that’s what keeps her going — her faith and her ability to block out negative energy. You feel like you know her, but she keeps all the things that are meaningful to her to herself."
However, Nick isn't interested in getting married again.
He said: "I don’t like the government in my love life. I think the institution of marriage should be respected, but I can’t see myself going through the legal paperwork again."
The 45-year-old star is known for his colourful personal life because, as well as Moroccan and Monroe, he is also a father to Golden, nine, Powerful, five, and Rise, four, with Brittany Bell; five-year-old twins Zion and Zillion, and Beautiful, three, with Abby De La Rosa; Legendary, four, with Bre Tiesi; Onyx, four, with LaNisha Cole; and Halo, three, with Alyssa Scott, the mom of his late son Zen, who died of cancer aged just five months in 2021.
While Nick doesn't have a "favourite" among the moms of his children, he admitted he has a particularly special bond with Bre.
Asked if he and Bre are together, he said: "I’m gonna take this opportunity to clear this up because I get in trouble a lot.
"The person who understands me the most would be Bre. We call each other twin flames because she accepts all of my s***, and I accept [her].
"There’s a sense of understanding I don’t have with anybody else. She’s super protective of me. You can’t buy that type of loyalty.
"She believes I should have a hierarchy system.
"As much as I say I don’t have a favourite, she definitely holds a special place in my heart."

item.content:encoded:
Courtney Green is taking "a break" from The Only Way Is Essex.
The 31-year-old reality TV star is set to take a step back from The Only Way Is Essex, after ten years on the ITV show.
A source told The Sun newspaper: "Courtney has decided to take a break from Towie ahead of a busy time for her family and across her business ventures.
"After the last series she just decided that a break and a reset would be beneficial for her in all sorts of ways. But she’ll be back – this isn’t goodbye – she’s just opting for some time out."
Courtney split from businessman Callum Bushby in 2025, after a seven-year relationship.
The reality star first split from Callum in 2019, because he wasn't ready to settle down at the time.
A source told The Sun Online at the time: "Courtney has her heart set on getting married to Callum and having children with him.
"All her friends have started to have babies and it’s made her start thinking about her own future."
Courtney and Callum were reported to have had different priorities at the time.
The insider explained: "She wanted him to show commitment and move in together, but he didn’t want to. He’s only young and is still enjoying going out with friends with no strings attached.
"Courtney ended things, but she’s adamant he’ll come crawling back. She’s been going out with her friends and having fun to take her mind off the split, but Callum’s got no intention of getting back together."
Callum always remained off-screen because he wasn't keen to appear on The Only Way Is Essex.
The businessman "hated the idea of being on the show" and he didn't wish to be "judged" by TV viewers.
The source said: "He just wasn’t comfortable with being famous. He hated the idea of being on the show with Courtney and having their relationship judged on-screen."

item.content:encoded:
90 Day: The Last Resort Season 3 was one of the messiest iterations of the spinoff yet, with many 90 Day Fiancé couples at a breaking point in their marriage. As the show rounds out its time on the 2026 TV schedule, I'm sure many are wondering what's going on with them in the present and if any of their marriages survived the trials and ghosts of the castle.
We learned a lot during the first part of the tell-all, and I was happy to see Ross Matthews back as host to ask some of the hard questions. There's even some additional info to share based on what we've seen on social media, so let's dive in and give an update on where things stand.
Jenny And Sumit - Still Together
Jenny and Sumit Singh went into 90 Day: The Last Resort after a failed business endeavor in which they tried to open a cafe. In addition to being out of money, they had no means to move out of the home he shared with his parents. Jenny was tired of living with them, but Sumit was torn about breaking the tradition of living in a blended family household.
Since the tell-all was filmed, Jenny confirmed that Sumit's parents moved out. We also learned that she was diagnosed with ALS, and there are plans in place for her to seek treatment in the United States. Unfortunately, Sumit has had trouble obtaining a visa to be with her, and until that happens, Jenny seemingly wants to remain in India until he can travel with her. Here's hoping they can get some help soon.
Guillermo And Kara - No Longer Together
Kara Leona and Guillermo Rojer weren't together when they joined 90 Day: The Last Resort, but there was hope from at least one of them that they could salvage their marriage. Unfortunately, they were unable to reach a compromise when it came to Kara's explicit online content, and he ended up leaving the resort before the recommitment ceremony and left a letter saying that he couldn't make things work.
They continue to co-parent in the present, but the odds of them getting back together feel as though they are slim to none. Again, I can't say I'm surprised, because I already assumed the marriage was over before this season began, so it was more just further confirmation. We also know that Kara will appear in the spinoff 90 Day: Hunt For Love, so there's a possibility she'll continue to be involved in the franchise for a long time.
Russ And Pao - No Longer Together
Russ and Pao Mayfield were struggling in their marriage, as the latter wrestled with feeling she didn't have the support of a strong husband to lead their family. She felt as though she was doing most everything on her own, and he began to feel like an unnecessary component in her life. Despite that, they found some common ground and ultimately recommitted after he signed a contract freeing them from the responsibility of his financial issues.
Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News
A few weeks ago, Pao announced a split from Russ. It doesn't look like they'll reconcile either, but until the papers are officially signed, one can never say for sure. I felt they had the best chance of staying married out of everyone involved, but I guess it wasn't meant to be.
Shekinah And Sarper - No Longer Together
Shekinah and Sarper Güven were the highlight couple of the season, with the collapse of their marriage playing out in real time. Things really went downhill after Shekinah made an offensive comment to Thaís Ramone, and it felt like the arguments between them only escalated.
Their marital issues have continued to play out on social media, with Shekinah claiming Sarper is making offensive jokes about her in his stand-up comedy, and fans saying they're seeing him date others while on tour. Shekinah skipped coming to the tell-all, and it seems plausible we may never see her in 90 Day Fiancé again. As for Sarper, there are reports that he's filmed an additional spinoff appearance alongside Tyray Mollett, and I can't wait to see what that's about.
Patrick And Thaís - No Longer Together
Patrick Mendez and Thaís Ramone were going through a rough patch in their marriage, but it seemed they were one of the only couples who saw effective progress through marriage counseling. Granted, some would say there's no greater unifier between a couple than a shared enemy, and they both found that when Shekinah got into a fight with them.
As we learned during the 90 Day: The Last Resort tell-all, Patrick and Thaís filed for divorce. There was even some shock amongst the fandom when the details behind a domestic dispute came to light, though the charges were ultimately dropped. They ultimately decided the fighting in front of their daughter was not setting a good example, and it was best to split rather than let her see that.
Rebecca And Zied - No Longer Together
Zied Hakimi and Rebecca Parrott's troubles have been the same since they first arrived on 90 Day Fiancé, and The Last Resort didn't change anything. Rebecca was still convinced that Zied cheated on her, but had no solid evidence to prove it. Zied attempted to ease her fears after letting her look through his phone, but her constant need to do so made him feel trapped in the marriage.
We don't have explicit confirmation that Rebecca and Zied are no longer together, though it's heavily suspected following comments by her daughter-in-law suggesting they've split. Rebecca hasn't posted on Instagram since July, and Zied doesn't have any recent pictures of them together on his social media. I think it's safe to say either Rebecca's suspicions panned out, or maybe Zied just grew tired of constantly being accused of doing nothing.
90 Day: The Last Resort's episodes at the castle are over, but the drama lives on forever over on HBO Max. For those who haven't watched, it's certainly worth the time for anyone looking for some fun reality television.
Mick Joest is a Content Producer for CinemaBlend with his hand in an eclectic mix of television goodness. Star Trek is his main jam, but he also regularly reports on happenings in the world of Star Trek, WWE, Doctor Who, 90 Day Fiancé, Quantum Leap, and Big Brother. He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

A game of truth or dare led high school best friends Bella Pepin and Cameron Kenny to realize they should be something more. “But my junior year and his senior year, everything changed,” Bella recalls. The two were dared to kiss each other at a Halloween party, and they automatically felt a spark. “We started dating pretty much immediately and dated through the rest of high school and throughout college with a few on-and-offs,” says Bella. After college, the two Florida natives drifted apart and didn’t see each other for five years. A chance meeting at a bar out in Montauk changed their fate. “We were too nervous to say hi to each other for over an hour or so,” she shares. “Eventually, we briefly chatted, but nothing came of that night!” Back in NYC, Bella decided to be forward and ask Cameron to grab coffee. “We ended up walking six miles in circles on the West Side Highway, catching up on the last five years of life. It felt like we picked back up right where we left off,” she shares. “We were so young when we first dated, so the time apart really allowed us to grow up and learn ourselves. Getting back together this time, we both knew it was for good.”
Two years later, the couple moved in together in Dallas with a golden retriever named Goose and a cat named Rigatoni. The following spring, Cameron proposed to Bella on his 31st birthday while they were on a trip together on Harbour Island, a place he has traveled to with his family for years. “He waited until the second night of the trip to propose—which really threw me off,” says Bella. The two were walking on the beach to dinner at sunset when Cameron popped the question as a hidden photographer captured the moment. The two continued the night with celebrations at dinner and calls with their families to tell them the news. “That same weekend, Cameron wasted no time and surprised me with a tour of The Other Side—our wedding venue,” says Bella. “It was full speed ahead!”
The two decided to have their friends and family join them for their Bahamas destination wedding on April 11, 2026. “There is something really special about it,” Bella says of Harbour Island. “We love the relaxed yet refined vibe, the food, the design, and the people… We never considered a wedding anywhere else.” Bella, who works as an interior designer, partnered up with their wedding planner Sophia Goff to execute their vision. “Sophia is a creative genius, and we immediately clicked,” she says. “Knowing how much I cared, she let me into the weeds with her—reviewing fabric samples and tabletop tailoring details and so much more. I’m so grateful she brought me behind the scenes.” The groom gives the two all the credit. Cameron adds, “I only helped manage the band and requested no lines at any bars!”
The vision for the weekend was to have a unique, elevated design perspective, without it feeling too serious. “Island-y, but not beach-y,” explains Bella. “All of our events were outdoors—with the exception of a rehearsal dinner pivot due to rain—so we wanted the designs to mimic natural Caribbean elements, sticking to a color and material palette seen in the surrounding tropical landscape.” The bride also put particular care into the invitations and paper goods throughout the weekend, hiring calligrapher Emily Snyder to create playful illustrations for the designs. The bride adds, “The kissing fish she doodled are everything to me!”
This design ethos also translated into Bella’s style choices for the weekend. “I wanted my wardrobe to feel classic, yet fun with loads of island influence,” she says. “The location lent itself to lots of texture and fun accessorizing—raffia fringe, sheer materials, floral appliqués, pearls, shells, and fish!” The bride credits her friend, stylist Madison Childs Lee, as a major help in curating her weekend ensembles. “She innately has a really cool eye, is a master at sourcing unique pieces, and helped me pull together the final touches on each look,” Bella shares.
The bride kicked off the weekend in a Danielle Frankel gown with hand-painted appliqués and baroque pearl tendrils for the rehearsal dinner. “I felt like a mermaid that just came from the sea,” she reminisces. For the beach day, Bella donned a sheer, lacework dress from Matin’s fall collection. She adds, “I think I saw a runway photo of it on their Instagram, and knew I needed it for the weekend!” The welcome party look by Holli Studio was one of the bride’s favorites. “The butter leather top and skirt with raffia fringe didn’t feel overly bridal and were so fun and flirty to wear,” she says. “I can't wait to rewear it.” Bella paired the set with a silver and pearl shell necklace her mom bought on her honeymoon in St. Croix in the ’80s. “Immediate prized possession status,” she adds.
For her trip down the aisle, the bride wore Danielle Frankel’s Arlo gown, a high-neck silk wool dress with pearl-like sheen, a low back, and raw chiffon trim. “I knew I wanted to be a Danielle Frankel bride, so much so that I didn’t try on any other bridal lines,” she says. “I worked with the team at the NYC studio on custom additions, and we ended up adding more of the raw chiffon material around the bust and down the waist. I love the added texture and airiness it gave the look.” She paired the look with a custom shell pouch from the brand by Sloan and custom diamond and pearl earrings by her friend Lili George made to mimic an Art Deco pair she once saw at an estate sale. “They added a touch of old-world to the look and I’ll cherish them forever,” Bella gushes.
Cameron kept his wedding weekend looks classic in custom suiting by P Johnson and Sid Mashburn. Tones of the looks were in blues, greens, and neutrals to mirror the design palette. “For the wedding day, he wanted to wear an ivory dinner jacket as a nod to what he wore when he took me to his senior prom,” shares Bella. “He wore cufflinks engraved with our initials gifted by me on wedding day, and black raffia loafers to give the look a bit more of an island feel.” She adds, “He looked so handsome.”
The weekend kicked off with a rehearsal dinner filled with speeches and classic Bahamian dishes served family style. “The interior design style of Pink Sands Hotel feels very British West Indies, so we leaned in,” shares the bride. “We had to move the dinner from their garden into the restaurant at the last minute due to rain, but I honestly think being inside the hotel gave more context to our design.” The night ended at a dive bar named Gusty’s complete with a disco ball and never-ending early-2000s hits. “We stayed out later than planned, but it was so much fun,” says Bella.
The following day, guests hit the beach at Ms. V’s and enjoyed painkillers, local beer, and fish sandwiches. “It was so fun to be hanging on the beach, sunning and swimming with all of our people in a more casual setting before the wedding events kicked off,” shares the bride. That night, the welcome party at Coral Sands Hotel’s Beach Bar was a “full-on shell explosion.” Custom coasters, aprons, menus, and mosaics all featured shell motifs. “We wanted to be super playful to go with the loud and punchy decor of the hotel,” Bella says.
The bride and groom spurred tradition and saw each other the morning of the wedding for a sunrise swim in the ocean. “It was the highlight of the weekend for me,” shares Bella. “Break the rules! See each other before the wedding!” As the ceremony approached, windy weather led to some last-minute changes. “I started with my hair styled down and 10 minutes before walking down the aisle, Alejandra threw it up into a bun,” says the bride. “We also ended up flipping the ceremony seating so guests were facing away from the ocean to avoid wind feedback on the mic. You can only plan for so much!”
The couple legally tied the knot in their hometown in Florida five months earlier, which helped shed some of the nerves around the ceremony. “I think we both felt more excited than nervous,” says the bride. “Cameron’s uncle Davis officiated, and we recited our own personal vows, which were very teary. How can you put a 15-year-long journey into two minutes?!” The newlyweds recessed to “Oh La La” by Faces and felt like they were in a movie. “We had a sweet moment to ourselves and cheersed with a spritz before joining the guests at cocktails on the lawn,” remembers Bella.
The cocktail and reception spaces were filled with native plants and overgrown florals. “The Other Side has a very weathered and wild vibe to it, and Sophia and I kept coming back to this idea of a deserted island,” says Bella. “But, of course, [we had] a really chic dressed-up dinner with silk taffeta table linens for a bit of unexpected fancy. It was black tie after all.”
Before dinner, the couple shared their first dance to “Cruisin’” by Smokey Robinson. “My mom raised my sisters and I on soul and Motown, and I’ve always loved this song. But now it holds a bigger meaning for us,” says the bride. Cameron danced to “In My Life” by The Beatles with his mother, and Bella’s father gave a speech with a Phil Collins-inspired intro. “It was nothing short of iconic, and got the crowd on their feet,” she shares.
The bride changed into a TWP strapless dress and shell necklace as the dancing really kicked off. The band played a curated setlist that kept the dance floor packed all night. Cameron notes, “It was electric!” The night transitioned to the after-party complete with a DJ and live saxophone player. “The groomsmen had my dad on their shoulders at one point, and even my 11-year-old sister stayed ‘til the early morning hours,” says Bella. “We never wanted it to end!”
Reflecting on the weekend, the bride says, “We’re just so happy, and everything felt so authentically us: the design, place, the music, our people, all of it.” Adds the groom, “I wouldn’t change a thing! I wish we could do it all again.”
